analysis.one_liner: Lets Americans import cheaper prescription drugs from Canada, the UK, Europe, and Switzerland.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in June 2024 with 8 cosponsors, all Democrats, and died in the House Energy and Commerce Committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite federal drug law to let licensed pharmacies, wholesalers, and individual patients buy qualifying prescription drugs from certified sellers in Canada, the United Kingdom, the European Union, and Switzerland — countries where the same drugs routinely sell for far less. It requires the government to certify those foreign sellers, test imported drugs for authenticity, and ban manufacturers from charging sellers more to block importation or from tweaking formulas to dodge it. The bill never got past its referral to committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Americans who skip or ration prescriptions because of cost, and pharmacies and wholesalers who could source lower-priced drugs abroad. The bill's own findings cite that US drug prices average 2.78 times comparable OECD countries, and that tens of millions of Americans have chosen not to fill a prescription due to cost [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Allows individuals to personally import up to a 90-day supply of a qualifying prescription drug from a certified foreign pharmacy with a valid US prescription, including insulin and dialysis solution [S2].
Permits wholesale distributors and pharmacies to import qualifying drugs, which could push down what consumers pay at the counter [S2].
Makes it illegal for a manufacturer to charge certified foreign sellers a higher price, restrict their supply, or change the US formulation specifically to defeat importation [S2].

Builds in safety controls: HHS certification of foreign sellers, approved-lab testing for chemical authenticity, importation tracing, recall notification, and suspension of importation where counterfeits or violations appear [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers, whose US prices would face new competition from cheaper versions of the same drugs sold abroad; they also bear the cost of complying with anti-discrimination and anti-circumvention rules [S2].

drawbacks.text: Importation adds safety and supply-chain risks: even with certification and testing, oversight of foreign online sellers is hard, and counterfeit or improperly handled drugs could reach patients through personal importation — a concern the FDA has long raised with broad importation schemes.

Savings for consumers are not guaranteed: importation programs require significant government administration (certification, testing, tracing, fees to fund enforcement), and manufacturers could legally raise foreign prices, since the anti-discrimination ban compares prices within the exporting country, not against US prices [S2].
Pharmaceutical manufacturers argue that lower US revenues would reduce the industry's research and development spending on new medicines — a trade-off an honest supporter must acknowledge.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real, well-documented problem — Americans paying several times what people in peer countries pay for identical drugs — and it does so with unusually detailed safety machinery (certification, testing, tracing, suspension powers) plus new criminal penalties for counterfeit online sellers. The genuine risks are enforcement complexity, uncertain consumer savings if manufacturers adjust foreign prices, and the acknowledged trade-off with drug-maker research revenue. On balance it is a serious, safeguards-heavy attempt at consumer savings, not a loose personal-importation free-for-all.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jan Schakowsky introduced the bill on June 26, 2024, with seven Democratic cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day [S1][S4].
That committee referral was the only action the bill ever received; no further action appears in its history before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S4].
Support was modest and entirely partisan: all 8 cosponsors were House Democrats, none from the 224 House Republicans [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers, who keep the protected American market where the same drugs sell at far higher prices; the bill died without costing them anything.

for.name: Rep. Jan Schakowsky
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Affordable and Safe Prescription Drug Importation Act of 2024 and referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee.

for.name: 8 of 216 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill: Reps. Cohen, Doggett, Grijalva, Norton, Omar, Pingree, and Pocan joined Schakowsky.

for.name: Pharmaceutical industry
for.what_they_did: The industry has a long, well-documented record of lobbying against drug importation proposals, arguing they compromise safety and threaten research funding.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by Rep. Cathy McMorris Rodgers (R-WA)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote was scheduled before the Congress ended.

against.name: House Republicans
against.what_they_did: None of the 224 House Republicans cosponsored the bill, and the Republican-controlled committee and floor agenda never took it up.

sides.party_line_note: All 8 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican ever backed the bill, which died in a committee chaired by a Republican in the Republican-controlled House.

industries.note: Importation would expose their protected US prices to competition from identical drugs sold much cheaper abroad, and the bill bans common manufacturer tactics — supply restrictions and formula changes — used to defeat importation. Their loss is the mechanism by which consumers would save.

industries.industry: Licensed foreign pharmacies and wholesale distributors in Canada, the UK, EU, and Switzerland
industries.note: The bill creates a new, certified export market for these sellers, paid for by certification fees that fund the program's administration. Their business opportunity depends on keeping imports safe, which aligns with the public's interest in genuine, effective drugs.

industries.industry: Pharmacies and wholesale distributors in the US
industries.note: US pharmacies and wholesalers could import cheaper qualifying drugs and potentially lower their costs, but those savings only reach consumers if competition and pricing transmit them, and importers take on new reporting and compliance duties.
